title: Sales Call Conversions
context: Two sales reps each make 25 calls in a day. Rep A is new (p = 0.30 of converting a call into a sale). Rep B is experienced (p = 0.68). A rep has a "strong day" if more than half of the 25 calls convert, i.e. at least 13 conversions. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Rep A's probability of converting all 25 calls is greater than 0.0000001%.
The probability that Rep A has a strong day is greater than the probability of exactly 13.
Rep B is more than 50 times as likely as Rep A to have a strong day.
Rep A's variance in number of conversions is greater than Rep B's variance.
The expected number of conversions for Rep B is more than double that of Rep A.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side A, $p = 0.3$ and $n = 25$:

$$P(X = 25) = (0.3)^{25}$$

$$\approx 0 \approx 8.4729 \times 10^{-12}\%$$

The claim compares this with $1 \times 10^{-7}\%$. We got about $8.4729 \times 10^{-12}\%$, which is below the cutoff, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

The named event covers every admissible count from 13 through 25, not only the single count 13. Those extra counts have positive probability when $0<p<1$, so the event probability is strictly larger than $P(X=13)$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli trials with success probability $p$. Each trial has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $n_A = 25$, $p_A = 0.3$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 25 \cdot 0.3 \cdot 0.7 = 5.25$$

Side B with $n_B = 25$, $p_B = 0.68$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 25 \cdot 0.68 \cdot 0.32 = 5.44$$

So $\mathrm{Var}(A) = 5.25$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B) = 5.44$.

The claim’s comparison is incorrect, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli trials each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 25 \cdot 0.3 = 7.5$$

$$E[B] = 25 \cdot 0.68 = 17$$

The mean ratio (B relative to A) is

$$\frac{E[B]}{E[A]} = \frac{17}{7.5} \approx 2.2667$$

(Double would mean a ratio of $2$.)

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Two sales reps each make 25 calls in a day. Rep A is new (p = 0.30 of converting a call into a sale). Rep B is experienced (p = 0.68). A rep has a "strong day" if more than half of the 25 calls convert, i.e. at least 13 conversions.

We model each side as a binomial count with $n = 25$ independent trials: side A has success probability $p_A = 0.3$, side B has $p_B = 0.68$.

The scenario’s success cutoff is at least $k = 13$ successes out of $n = 25$.
